Swagger

SWAG-er -- likely from an old dialect word 'swag,' meaning to sway unsteadily. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Swagger is a confident and arrogant way of walking.

The rookie walked into the locker room with a swagger that annoyed even his own teammates.

Worked Example

A newly crowned champion strolls into the press conference with his shoulders back and his chin raised, clearly enjoying every eye in the room.

That cocky, self-assured way of moving through a room is exactly what swagger describes. Unlike 'shuffle,' which suggests hesitation, swagger announces confidence -- sometimes too much of it.

How Swagger Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

strut

strut: to walk in a proud, self-important way

bravado

bravado: a bold, showy display of confidence

cockiness

cockiness: an excessive, overconfident self-assurance

Antonyms

meekness

meekness: a quiet, humble, unassuming manner

timidity

timidity: a lack of courage or confidence

How Strong Is It? — strut → swagger → bravado

strut vs. swagger

strut vs. swagger: Strut is close to swagger, though swagger more specifically implies an arrogant edge, while a strut can sometimes be simple showing off without any hint of attitude.

bravado vs. swagger

bravado vs. swagger: Bravado can feel bigger than swagger: swagger is mostly about how someone walks or carries themselves, while bravado can extend to loud words and bold claims, not just body language.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Swagger likely grew out of an old dialect word swag, 'to sway or lurch,' with the -er ending that marks repeated action, as in flutter and stagger. To swagger is to walk with a repeated, showy sway.

Use the root in a new word: swag

Use the root in a new word: swag: Everyone at the conference lined up early to grab a bag of free swag from the sponsor booths.
